data.title: Hradište near Partizánske – a hillfort above the Nitrica
data.excerpt: A hillfort of 6.45 ha guards the narrowest point of the Nitrica valley above the right bank of the river; on the open western side it is closed by a rampart some 400 m long and 5 m high. It was most probably built by the people of the Lusatian culture and used again by the Slavs in the 9th–10th centuries; today the Romanesque church of St Barnabas and its cemetery stand on it.
data.metaTitle: Hradište near Partizánske – a hillfort above the Nitrica
data.metaDescription: An upland hillfort of 6.45 ha above the Nitrica, built by the Lusatian culture and later used by the Slavs. Štefan Janšák measured it in 1928.

children.text: The upland hillfort at Hradište is a natural formation situated at the narrowest point of the Nitrica valley, on the right bank of the river Nitrica. Geologically, the smaller part of the hillfort, called Pravdová, is formed on its northern and north-eastern sides by inaccessible dolomitic limestones. The greater part of the hillfort’s enclosure consists of a sandy substratum. It is covered by clayey-sandy and clayey soil, which today serves as arable land.

The sandy substratum on the southern side of the hillfort was used more extensively as building material. When the quarrying of sand came close to the church, further work was prohibited for safety reasons. The layer of soil above the sandy substratum varies in thickness. In some places deep ploughing turns up stones. In prehistory the hillfort served as a settlement of human communities. It had a defensive function and was inaccessible from three sides. On the open side the defence of the hill was strengthened by an earthen rampart, the remains of which have survived to this day.

blocks.alt: Aerial view of the Hradište hillfort (near Partizánske)

children.text: The hillfort lies at an elevation of 210 m above sea level, its highest point being 260 m. It has an uneven, saddle-shaped surface running in an east–west direction. The area of the hillfort, the smaller part of which is covered by turf, is used for grazing cattle. A smaller area is built over by the church, and the old and the new cemetery are situated close to it. The largest part of the hillfort’s enclosure serves as arable land.

. The village is an example of an old settlement that is not recorded in written sources. It is first mentioned only in 1533, even though the Romanesque church of St Barnabas, built around the year 1100, stands on the hillfort, with a preserved cemetery around it containing gravestones of the
11th and 12th centuries.
The Romanesque font is currently held in the Slovak National Museum – Bojnice Castle.
The height and area parameters were measured in 1928 by Ing. Janšák, the founder of Slovak archaeology, a historian and teacher. Janšák describes the hillfort as follows:

blocks.text: The hillfort at Hradište extends on an upper projection (a promontory) above the village of Hradište, by the Veľké Bielice–Vestenice highway, Nitra County. One side is a rock of friable limestone, broken up by mountain pressure, disintegrating into gravel and sand and therefore torn by heavy rains into crumbling gullies. The highest-lying part of the hillfort is a steep rock of calcareous tufa, rising above the level of the road. The third side is a gently inclined pasture, cut through by gullies and overgrown with shrubs. Part of this side is arable field. By its geographical position the hillfort lies on a mountain projection or promontory. The western side is therefore the least protected by nature, being connected with the rest of the terrain by an open and very flat ridge. It is provided with a strong rampart about 400 m long and 5 m high at its highest point. Its cross-section is 60 m wide at the base. This slope is today probably considerably lower than its original height, because cultivated fields lie upon it. As a consequence, with every ploughing the soil is moved down from the top of the rampart in both directions.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.text: The rampart is constantly being flattened and becoming lower. How much of its original height has been lost in this way cannot even be approximately stated. If we consider that the rampart still carried timber palisades on its crest, a walkway about 2 m wide was needed in case defence became necessary. It may be assumed that on the outer side the rampart was 10 m wide and that the inner side, along which there had to be free access to the palisades, had a gentler slope. Along its whole length the rampart is preserved very distinctly and at first sight gives the impression of a great natural wave in the terrain. Only after careful observation can it be established that it was made by human hand. At its end it is interrupted by a road cutting into it. The surface of the hillfort is divided into two large parts with a total surface area of 6.45 ha. The first part, which lies on the elevated spot and is the best protected and therefore the safest, was the place where both the secular and the spiritual chiefs and leaders resided. By its position and importance it could be regarded as a kind of acropolis. In the second part of the hillfort lies the cemetery, in which burials still take place today.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

blocks.alt: Aerial view of the Hradište hillfort (near Partizánske)

blocks.text: To the north of the cemetery stands the church, enclosed by a wall, and it may be assumed that in the places where the church stands today there were once pagan altars at which the earliest inhabitants offered gifts to their gods. The transition from paganism to Christianity was not as sudden as history textbooks present it. The disputes between the adherents of Christianity and of the original paganism were often overcome slowly and perhaps harshly as well. The new Christian teaching gradually settled into the hearts of the faithful. Those who accepted the Christian faith changed not only inwardly but also outwardly; the outward changes were manifested in their seats and dwellings. The Christians gradually rid themselves of pagan customs and superstitions. The finds were recorded only on the surface, without excavation; they are sherds of the first Iron Age, scattered over the whole surface of the hillfort, chiefly however in its eastern half. Massed finds of sherds were made in the places where the ramparts had been dug into and were slipping down the slope. This would suggest that the ramparts were repaired and added to several times and that the remains of vessels thus came to be in them. On that side there are open quarries, and from them the hillfort is threatened with great damage. There were no excavations, neither trial nor systematic ones; indeed, this hillfort is not mentioned anywhere in the specialist literature. In the cemetery, in freshly dug graves, there are no occupation layers, and not even sherds were found. At that spot the soil is very hard, mixed with coarse gravel and boulders. In places the rocks lie close to the surface, to which the started and unfinished graves that had to be dug elsewhere bear witness. The hillfort was discovered by the author in August of the year 1926.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

children.text: This is an abridged text of the article that was published in the proceedings of the museum society in 1928. In the article the author wrote that Slavic prehistoric hillforts, or hillforts from the dawn of historical times, generally lie on the projections of mountain ranges, on the boundary between the uplands and the plain or the valley adjoining them. The hillfort at Hradište had a defensive and an economic significance. The description of the hillfort is in many respects stimulating for archaeological and historical research. To this day the hillfort has not been comprehensively investigated by archaeology. Nor has the significance and position of the hillfort in the Slavic period yet been unambiguously determined. All the finds made on the surface of the hillfort come from surface collection or from chance turning-up by farmers’ ploughs.

blocks.alt: Plan of the hillfort after Š. Janšák (1928)

children.text: Hallstatt material
(the Lusatian culture) occurred all over the hillfort. At the locality known as Pravdová a settlement horizon was located, dating from the
11th to the 14th–15th centuries.

This locality forms only part of the Hallstatt settlement area. Geophysical survey (A. Ruttkay) suggests the existence of a building on the edge of the acropolis, which has not been investigated. It may be the property of the Hospitaller convent of King Stephen in Esztergom, which is mentioned in two charters, but its precise identification is not certain.
The medieval castle

In ancient times a castle or a castle-like structure stood on Pravdová. The castle was the property of a magnate who bore the Old Slavic name Pravda. The mention of the castle and its owner is given in the lexicon Magyar országh varmegy (Nyitra), where it is written that in the 15th century the ruin of a castle stood at Hradište on the hill above the settlement. The remains of the foundations of the structure were visible in the 1930s on the edge of the rise of the hillfort facing south-west. In later years the remains of the masonry were covered by the turf that forms the surface of the rise.
And we shall add one more legend:

blocks.alt: Section through the hillfort after Š. Janšák (1928)

children.text: According to an old legend handed down from generation to generation in the village of Hradište, a castle stood on Pravdová in which there lived a magnate named Pravdapán, who owned the settlement below the castle and the fields and forests in the immediate surroundings. There was also a castle on the hill of Chotoma on the left bank of the Nitrica. Another magnate lived there – Chotomapán, who owned all the forests and settlements to the north of Hradište. The two magnates maintained a link with each other across a suspension bridge that joined Pravdová with Chotoma. The bridge was necessary because between the castles lay impassable country filled with marshes and primeval floodplain forest. The legend of the suspension bridge lacks a rational core. Given the level of technical possibilities of the time, such a structure could not have been built.
